facts.text: Ray tracing simulates a sensor by following imaginary light, radio or sound rays into a virtual scene, bouncing them off surfaces and recording returns; shooting-and-bouncing rays (SBR) is the radar version that launches many rays and sums their reflections.
facts.quote: Ray tracing simulates a sensor by following imaginary rays of light, radio or sound from the sensor into the virtual scene, bouncing them off surfaces and recording what comes back; shooting-and-bouncing rays is the radar version that launches very many rays and adds up their reflections.

facts.text: Radar shooting-and-bouncing rays (SBR) follows multiple bounces between the machine body, ground and nearby structures and sums the results, allowing multipath ghosts and Doppler shifts to appear naturally.
facts.quote: lets each bounce several times between the machine body, the ground and nearby structures, and sums the results, so multipath ghosts and Doppler shifts appear naturally.

facts.text: Full-wave solvers compute electromagnetic physics exactly but are far too slow to simulate a whole quarry.
facts.quote: Full-wave solvers compute the electromagnetic physics exactly but are far too slow for a whole quarry [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Ray tracing is the core of the physics-based sensor-model family, and ray-traced lidar using the real scan pattern and signal chain is the best-validated sensor model type.
facts.quote: Ray tracing is the core of the physics-based sensor-model family, and ray-traced lidar with the real scan pattern and signal chain is the best-validated model type [Chapter 6].

facts.text: A one-hit radar model that treats each ray strike as a detection misses multipath and material behavior; a ray-traced material model produced far closer real and synthetic images.
facts.quote: For radar, a one-hit model that treats each ray strike as a detection misses multipath and material behavior, whereas a ray-traced material model produced far closer real and synthetic images [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Ray tracing responds causally to changes in geometry, materials, weather and sensor position, allowing extrapolation to new machines and mounting positions that learned models cannot perform well.
facts.quote: Ray tracing responds causally to changed geometry, materials, weather and sensor position, so it can extrapolate to new machines and mounting positions, which learned models cannot do well

facts.text: Ray tracing needs supplier internals and material data.
facts.quote: but it needs supplier internals and material data

facts.text: Ray-tracing errors grow in heavy precipitation.
facts.quote: its errors grow in heavy precipitation [Chapter 6].

facts.text: A CPU radar solver took 14 hours to simulate a 12-second scenario, illustrating ray-tracing costs that span orders of magnitude.
facts.quote: Cost spans orders of magnitude: a CPU radar solver took 14 hours for a 12-second scenario

facts.text: A vendor figure puts a GPU real-time radar solver at about 12 ms per frame.
facts.quote: a GPU real-time version takes about 12 ms per frame (a vendor figure)

facts.text: An independent radar ray tracer measured 7.8 to 18.8 ms per image on a consumer graphics card.
facts.quote: an independent radar ray tracer measured 7.8 to 18.8 ms per image on a consumer graphics card [Chapter 6].

facts.text: The reported CPU radar solver, GPU real-time radar solver and independent radar ray-tracer runtimes are examples, not planning constants.
facts.quote: These are examples, not planning constants [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Ray tracing is the method most likely to provide a trusted sensor model for a machine or mounting position never physically tested, addressing the program's core transfer problem, but only if the materials and sensor signal chain are known.
facts.quote: Ray tracing is the method most likely to give a sensor model that can be trusted on a machine or mounting position never physically tested, which is the core of the program's transfer problem, but only if the materials and the sensor's signal chain are known [Chapter 6].
